newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Afghanistan wants talks, says Taleban hit hard.
newsitem.headline: Afghanistan wants talks, says Taleban hit hard.

text.p: The Afghan government said on Wednesday it had caused heavy casualties among Taleban militia attacking Kabul and the capital was not about to fall, but that it nonetheless wanted a ceasefire and negotiations.
Afghan Deputy Foreign Minister Adbul Rahim Ghafoorzai made the remarks to reporters at the United Nations in New York as the U.N. Security Council met to discuss the crisis.
Ghafoorzai said Pakistani forces had helped the Taleban in their push toward the Afghan capital and said he would present evidence on this to the Security Council.
"We would like the Security Council to call on the Taleban and also their supporters to agree on a ceasefire and to a resolution of the conflict through peaceful means," he said.

The Taleban controls more than half of the central Asian country which has been the scene of continual fighting between various Moslem and ethnic groups since Soviet troops supporting a communist government withdrew in 1989.

The Taleban, who emerged from the obscurity of religious schools in Pakistan two years ago, have been fighting to oust President Burhanuddin Rabbani's government and impose a strict Islamic order across Afghanistan.
Earlier, a top U.N. official had said the radical Islamic group could be on the verge of taking Kabul as government resistance to their onslaught seeemed to be crumbling.
"The Taleban have been pushed back ... they have sustained heavy casualties ... Apparently, there is not any obvious danger to the security of Kabul," Ghafoorzai said.
Government forces had killed 150 fighters from the militant Islamic group, wounded 500 more and destroyed 18 tanks and 12 other vehicles in the Kabul fighting, he said.
U.N. Under-Secretary General for Political Affairs Marrack Goulding earlier told reporters there was little hope of negotiations between the Taleban and Rabbani's government.

"We are getting indications ... that Kabul may be on the point of falling," said Goulding, who is in touch with U.N. officials in Kabul. He visited the country last week to try to broker negotiations that would end the conflict.
The United Nations has appealed for an end to the fighting and for a negotiated settlement.
The Afghan government requested the U.N. Security Council meeting, saying in a letter that forces from neighbouring Pakistan had been involved in supporting the Islamist Taleban.
The Afghan government has often accused Pakistan of supporting the Taleban but Islamabad denies the charge. The Taleban have made spectacular military advances recently.
